source.title: The central nucleus of the amygdala and the construction of defensive modes across the threat-imminence continuum

confidence_rationale: Authoritative synthesis in a top venue proposing that the central amygdala uses mutually inhibitory, winner-takes-all circuits to switch between discrete defensive modes organised along threat imminence. Supports two structural commitments MECH-489 makes: that post-arrest action selection is a selection among mutually exclusive defensive modes (approach / withdraw / resume) rather than a continuous adjustment, and that phasic and chronic defensive states are architecturally distinct (the MECH-489 vs MECH-279 boundary). Confidence is 0.70 rather than higher because this is a review/perspective rather than a single decisive experiment, and because the organising variable it proposes -- threat imminence, learned through association -- is not the variable MECH-489 gates on.
failure_signatures: If defensive modes are selected by mutually inhibitory winner-takes-all competition, a decision layer that resolves to the same mode on every single override event is not exhibiting selection at all -- a winner-takes-all circuit with a structurally biased input produces exactly that degenerate signature.

Defensive mode is organised by threat imminence and prior association; a mechanism that gates only on instantaneous onset magnitude has no representation of imminence and so cannot reproduce the mode ordering the biology shows.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Laboratory paradigms eliciting rodent defensive responses reveal brain mechanisms underlying distinct threat-related behavioural modes. The central nucleus of the amygdala employs mutually inhibitory circuits with a winner-takes-all strategy to facilitate transitions between defensive responses, which are organised along a continuum of threat imminence and shaped by learned threat associations.
mapping.ree_translation: MECH-489's Components 4 and 5 resolve a post-arrest decision into approach, withdraw or resume by comparing harm and benefit channels. This paper supports the architectural shape of that: defensive action selection in the biology is discrete mode selection under mutual inhibition, not graded modulation, so a substrate that produces one of a small set of mutually exclusive behavioural modes is structurally right. It also supports MECH-489's registered boundary against MECH-279: modes at different points on the imminence continuum are constructed by different circuit configurations, which is what a phasic-arrest claim and a chronic-suffering-freeze claim being separate mechanisms would predict.
mapping.mapping_caveat: The organising variable differs, and this matters. The biology arranges defensive modes along THREAT IMMINENCE -- how close in space and time the threat is -- learned through association over experience. MECH-489 gates on an instantaneous onset derivative and then resolves via a harm-versus-benefit comparison at the current location. REE has no imminence representation, so the mapping is to the competitive-selection ARCHITECTURE only, not to the variable that drives it. This is also a review rather than a primary result: the winner-takes-all proposal is the authors' synthesis of a literature, and inherits whatever is unsettled in it. Rodent throughout.
mapping.source_context: Review and perspective synthesising rodent defensive-behaviour paradigms and central-amygdala circuit anatomy

confidence_components.notes: Source quality high: Nature Neuroscience perspective by established investigators in the field, synthesising a large and reasonably convergent rodent literature. Mapping fidelity moderate at 0.62 -- the competitive-selection architecture transfers well, the imminence organising variable does not transfer at all since REE has no analogue of it. Transfer risk 0.35: rodent to abstract agent, but the inference concerns a computational strategy (mutual inhibition, winner-takes-all) which is the kind of thing that does transfer across substrates more readily than anatomy does.
